common_name: Bruce's White Creeping Phlox (Pure White Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in early spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in dappled to full shade, spacing plants about a foot apart to let the stolons knit together quickly.

directions: Bruce's White is a free-flowering selection of creeping phlox prized for its clean, pure white blooms that stand out sharply against a low mat of semi-evergreen foliage in mid-spring. Like the species, it spreads by surface stolons that root as they travel, gradually forming a dense, weed-suppressing carpet beneath deciduous trees and along shaded woodland paths. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil and cool root conditions, since it fades in hot, dry summers and struggles south of zone 8. Shear lightly after bloom to tidy the mat and divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Home Fires Creeping Phlox (Rose-Pink Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants roughly a foot apart so the mat fills in within a season or two.

directions: Home Fires is a vigorous creeping phlox selection noted for its saturated rose-pink flowers, a warmer and more intense pink than most seedling-grown plants of the species produce. It forms a low, spreading mat of semi-evergreen foliage that roots along its stolons as it travels, making it useful for covering shaded slopes or filling gaps between larger woodland perennials. It flowers heavily in mid-spring and rebounds quickly after a post-bloom shearing, but like other P. stolonifera selections it needs reliably moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and cool summer shade to perform well. Divide every few years once the center of the patch begins to thin.

common_name: Blue Ridge Creeping Phlox (Blue-Violet Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to let the stolons establish before summer heat arrives.

directions: Blue Ridge is a robust creeping phlox cultivar selected for its clear blue-violet flowers, a cooler, truer blue than the lavender tones typical of wild populations. It builds a dense, semi-evergreen mat that spreads steadily by rooting stolons, making it a reliable groundcover for shaded banks, woodland garden edges, and the front of a shade border. It blooms profusely in mid-spring, but performs best with consistent moisture and cool, humus-rich soil, since hot, humid summers south of zone 8 can thin the planting. Cut back lightly after flowering to maintain a tight, tidy mat.

common_name: Pink Ridge Creeping Phlox (Rose-Pink Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, watering well until the mat is established.

directions: Pink Ridge is a creeping phlox selection bred as a pink-flowered companion to 'Blue Ridge', producing abundant clear rose-pink flowers over a low, spreading mat of semi-evergreen foliage in mid-spring. It roots along its stolons as it spreads, gradually forming a dense groundcover suited to shaded slopes, woodland paths, and the front edge of mixed shade plantings. Plant it in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade and keep it consistently watered through summer, since it is intolerant of prolonged drought or heavy heat. Divide congested patches every three to four years and shear lightly after bloom to encourage fresh growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, spacing closely since this selection stays unusually low and tight.

directions: Pierre is an unusually compact selection of green-and-gold, forming a tight, low mat of dark green foliage only a few inches tall that hugs the ground more closely than the species. It produces the same cheerful, five-petaled yellow, star-shaped flowers from mid-spring into summer, but in denser profusion relative to its small size, making it a good choice for edging shaded paths or tucking between stepping stones. Plant it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade and keep it evenly moist, especially during its first growing season, since it dries out faster than larger-leaved selections. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes and rarely needs division, though older patches can be lifted and replanted to rejuvenate a tired planting.
